Hi Liesl,

You need to install the version of dartR from CRAN. You need to install it in an RStudio session with an empty environment (no variables stored) otherwise the genlight objects that you created before will automatically load the dartR version you have already installed. You can either remove all the objects from your environment or create a new Rstudio project just to install the CRAN version.

To install the CRAN version, try:

install.packages("dartR")
library(dartR)
t1 <- platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>
gl.report.heterozygosity(t1)

Cheers,
Luis

See code below.

Cheers,
Luis

library(dartR)
#read function documentation
?gl.report.pa <http://gl.report.pa>
#private alleles/fixed differences report
res <- gl.report.pa <http://gl.report.pa>(platypus.gl <http://platypus.gl>, loc_names = TRUE)
#print results
res

messages.subject: PopGenR Question
messages.body_plain:
We have been asked what does a negative eigenvalue mean in a PCA? Negative eigenvalues are associated with eigenvectors directed in an imaginary (sensu sqrt(-1)) direction. In practice, negative eigenvalues mean that your distance matrix is not Euclidean and so cannot be faithfully represented in a space defined by Cartesian coordinates. This is of practical consequence only if the sum of the negative eigenvalues is approaching in magnitude the sum of the eigenvalues in your final representation, usually 2 or 3 dimensions. gl.pcoa() will provide the necessary diagnostics to make this judgement.

In summary, Legendre and Legendre and Gower recommend examining the eigenvalues and if there is a major issue with negative eigenvalues to consider better addressing poor callrate (missing values break metricity), using another distance measure, or applying a transformation.

Hope this helps.

Arthur

messages.body_plain:
Hi Laura,

Quite a few questions there. Pros and Cons of PCA versus PCoA. If the PCoA is performed with a Euclidean Distance matrix, then it is broadly equivalent to a PCA (which draws upon the covariance matrix). One difference is that classical PCA is intolerant of missing values and requires either some form of imputation or rather drastic pruning of your data. PCoA works with a distance matrix, and so with distances that deal with missing values between individuals in pairwise fashion.

DAPC combines PCA and discriminant function analysis to attenuate groupings. I am a little uncomfortable with this approach.

The factor loadings function reports the loci that load high with a particular PCA axis. Refer to the example in BioxRiv https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.03.22.533737 as to why you might want to do this. In that example, an inversion resulted in a serious distortion, that is, three groups that separated on axis 2. This was an artifact arising from what appeared to be a substantial structural variant in the skink genome (an inversion probably). To remove the artificial pattern, the loci that loaded high with axis 2 were removed from the analysis.

I will answer the sampling size question separately.

Hope this helps. Arthur

messages.subject: PopGenR Workshop Question #2
messages.body_plain:
Laura asked about the impact of unequal sample sizes on PCA.  Lets consider four populations that are equidistant to each other, the distances between them having arisen independently by drift. Three of these A, B and C, have sample sizes of 30 individuals and the fourth, D, has a sample size of 10.

It does not take much to realize that the distinction between A, B and C will be represented in the first two dimensions of the ordination (which you are most likely to examine), and the distinction of D will be relegated to the third dimension. In some instances, D may be overlaid by, say, B in the two dimensions. So sample size matters.

You could imagine a scenario, as Chris raised, of the two populations B and D being the most distinctive, but because of the low sample size for D, this greatest distinction will not be apparent in the first two dimensions. Equal sample sizes would resolve this distortion, though obviously examining more that 2 dimensions would resolve it too.

There has been a suggestion that the PCA visual representation of distances between
individuals is sensitive to sample size (Elhaik, 2022). But the sample size dependency identified by Elhaik arises because decreasing the sample size of one structural grouping (population, aggregation of populations, taxon) will reduce its contribution to overall variance and reorient the individuals in the space defined by the informative dimensions of the ordination. This leads to potentially dramatic changes in their projection on to the top two dimensions. Thus sample size effect can have major consequences for interpretation if the analyst's focus is restricted to two or three-dimensional PCA plots. The apparent lack of reproducibility identified by Elhaik (2022) arises from restricting attention to only the top two (or three) of informative dimensions. Misinterpretation arising from this effect can be overcome by appropriate examination of the ordination, including all substantial informative dimensions.

If that is not clear, consider the hypothetical example above and what would happen if you progressively increased the sample size of population D from 10 to 40 and concurrently population A from 30 to 25. This would cause the rotation of the PCA axes until we had differentiation of populations B, C and D in the top two dimensions, and population A relegated to the third. If you are only considering the first two dimensions of the ordination, your interpretation might change dramatically.

The lesson here is to be sure to examine all informative dimensions (those with substantial variance explained) before coming to conclusions. Look at the scree plot that is output by dartR, and then progressively look at those informative dimensions two at a time. Then you will not be fooled by the effect of sample size variation among your samples.

Hope this helps.

Arthur
Elhaik, E. (2022). Principal Component Analyses (PCA)-based findings in population genetic
studies are highly biased and must be re-evaluated. Scientific Reports, 12, 14683.
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-14395-4.

Refer also https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.03.22.533737

Hi everyone,
just a feedback on this issue.
I managed to figure out where the problem was, at least I think! :p

The problem emerged because I used a different computer (with a different Microsoft tools packages version) to install and test dartRverse.
When I tried to import the DArT .csv file with the dartRverse package installed in this new computer, I got the wrong reading of SNPs, as outlined in my message above.
So, I tried to install a previous version of dartR in a separate library folder on the same PC, to test whether the problem of importing properly the DArT object was within the new dartRverse package.
I installed dartR 2.7.2, but then I had the same problem: gl.read.dart read ~59000 SNPs instead of ~ 116000.

However, there was a warning message below:
"Warning message:
In scan(file = file, what = what, sep = sep, quote = quote, dec = dec,  :
    embedded nul(s) found in input"

So, when I googled this, it turns out it may be an incompatibility issue between .csv files imported with different versions of Excel, using different encoding methods (i.e. UTF-16LE) -->
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/23209464/get-embedded-nuls-found-in-input-when-reading-a-csv-using-read-csv

So, instead of reading the file that I had originally imported with the Excel version in my previous computer, I transferred in the new computer the original .csv file from DArT never opened before in my previous PC, and voila': dartR now reads 116000 SNPs - the correct number of SNPs.

I also tested dartRverse::dartR.base, like this:
dartR::gl.rad.dart(filename = "C:/myDArT.csv", ind.metafile = ("C:/myMetadata.csv") # --> and it reads the correct number of SNPs too! :)

I just wanted to let everyone know, in case by any chance you encounter the same or a similar problem!!

And for the dartR staff - sorry to have freaked you out!  dartR.base::gl.read.dart works fine! (at least for me!)

Thanks a lot!
Happy Easter
Gabry

messages.subject: Re: How to determine ld_max_pairwise for linkage disequilbrium
messages.subject_clean: How to determine ld_max_pairwise for linkage disequilbrium
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Here is the answer and logic that my lab came up with, to solve my problem. Hopefully it can be of help to others in the future.

I am pruning for LD for my parentage analysis. So, for my SNPs to be most informative I need all pairs of loci to be statistically independent of each other.

There are three "sources" of LD.
1) Physical linkage (the one that most people think of when considering LD). Two loci are physically close on the chromosome. Some of this linkage can addressed by removing secondaries (2 loci on the same tag), but not all.
2) A pair of loci may appear to be physically linked because a population has been strongly bottlenecked, with very few founding chromosomes. For example, if a few males are highly homozygous and are doing a lot of breeding, they are likely to pass these paired loci on to their offspring. This will look like LD in that population.
3) Epistatic selection where alleles in two or more loci that are far apart are inherited together because they give a selective advantage (e.g. rabbit immune systems need to have a pair of loci that are located on different chromosomes).

Filtering for LD for parentage analysis, we want to remove any loci pairs as defined 1-3.

To filter for LD gl.filter.ld(), you must first use gl.report.ld.map(). The help section of gl.report.ld.map() states that "If SNPs are mapped to a reference genome, the parameter ld_max_pairwise should be filled out (i.e. not NULL)." , where ld_max_pairwise = maximum distance in number of base pairs at which LD should be calculated. In my case, my SNPs are mapped to a reference genome. However, by including ld_max_pairwise parameter I would not remove linkage due to 3) epistatic selection. So, even though I have my loci mapped to a reference genome, I don’t want to use ld_max_pairwise.

Cheers,
Lana
